replacements.originalStem: Why does a freely falling water stream typically become narrower with increasing distance below a tap?
replacements.originalOptionB: Its speed increases while approximately the same water volume passes each level per
replacements.proposedStem: Why does a freely falling water stream typically become narrower with increasing distance below a tap?

proposedOptions.text: Its mass disappears during the fall
Its speed increases while approximately the same water volume passes each level per second
Its density must double after leaving the tap
Water particles slow down continuously while falling

replacements.explanation: Gravity accelerates a falling water stream. For approximately steady incompressible flow, the volume flow rate Q = Av is approximately constant, so a higher speed requires a smaller cross-sectional area.

replacements.originalStem: A main stream (area 2 cm2; speed 5 m s-1) divides into two equal branches of area 1 cm2 each. Branch speed is:
replacements.proposedStem: A main stream (area 2 cm2; speed 5 m s-1) divides into two equal branches of area 1 cm2 each, with equal volume flow rate through both branches. Speed in either branch is:
replacements.explanation: The 2 cm² inlet at 5 m/s carries 10 cm²·m/s. Equal volume discharge into two 1 cm² branches gives 2 × 1 × v = 10; hence v = 5 m/s per branch. Equal branch areas alone do not require equal discharge.
replacements.provenance: Source archived from original teacher-prepared bank; corrected practice wording approved by teacher.

replacements.originalStem: NBF Example 6.3: Aorta radius 0.8 cm, speed 0.33 m s-1; blood enters 30 arteries each radius 0.4 cm. Speed in each artery is:
replacements.proposedStem: Based on the idealized equal-flow split in NBF Example 6.3: Aorta radius 0.8 cm, speed 0.33 m s-1; blood enters 30 arteries, each of radius 0.4 cm, with equal volume flow through each artery. Speed in each artery is:
replacements.explanation: For the idealized equal-flow model based on NBF Example 6.3, A_in v_in = 30 A_out v_out, giving v_out = (0.8/0.4)² × 0.33 / 30 = 0.044 m/s. Equal radii alone do not prove equal discharge.
replacements.provenance: Printed NBF Example 6.3 numerical data/results verified in V95-C2S; clarified question wording is teacher-authored, not verbatim textbook text.

replacements.originalStem: One vessel (radius 1 cm) divides into 50 equal vessels (radius 0.1 cm). If initial speed is 0.20 m s-1 and flow is conserved, branch speed is:
replacements.proposedStem: One vessel (radius 1 cm) divides into 50 equal-radius vessels (radius 0.1 cm), with equal volume flow rate through each branch. If initial speed is 0.20 m s-1 and the fluid is approximately incompressible, speed in each branch is:
replacements.explanation: For steady incompressible flow divided equally among 50 outlets, π(1 cm)² × 0.20 m/s = 50π(0.1 cm)² × v. Therefore v = 0.40 m/s. Equal outlet radii without equal discharge do not uniquely determine individual speeds.
